Before you begin

1. Before you begin

Linux System Administration
From the Command Line to Production Infrastructure
Dr. Charles Dorner
First edition · 2026

Edition assembly note. This edition preserves the foundational Chapters 1–18 from the earlier manuscript and completes Chapters 19–33 against the supplied curriculum. The additional explanations, HarborWorks cases, capstone, reference directory, and appendices are newly composed teaching material. The earlier draft’s unfulfilled companion and reference mentions are completed here. Core example source is printed in the book; the companion supplies the same files and executable fixture tests.

A server can accept a command and still fail the people who depend on it. A backup job can exit successfully while saving the wrong directory. A service can be running while every customer receives an error. A firewall change can improve an audit score while locking out the only administrator. Linux administration begins with commands, but it becomes a profession when those commands are connected to evidence, responsibility, and recovery.

This book follows a fictional organization, HarborWorks, as it builds and operates a small Linux environment. The recurring service is HarborStatus, an internal status website. The examples are invented teaching scenarios, not descriptions of an employer’s systems. Their addresses, accounts, workloads, and service targets are examples unless explicitly identified otherwise. No confidential infrastructure details are used.

The book preserves a concept-first progression: understand the requirement, inspect the mechanism, make a bounded change, verify the result, and prove that recovery is possible. Every numbered topic in the 33-chapter curriculum has its own section. Each chapter also includes a worked example and a practice lab. The final two chapters bring the earlier material together through fault diagnosis and a complete server-build sequence.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch001.xhtml — About this edition

2. Read the operational contract

Keep the source procedure, its preconditions and its verification together. Follow the named primary documentation for the installed version. A command copied without its surrounding assumptions answers a different question.

SOURCE: Read the operational contract

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch001.xhtml — About this edition

5. Technical scope

The primary teaching baselines are Ubuntu Server 24.04 LTS and the RHEL 9 family, including Rocky Linux 9 and AlmaLinux 9. These are deliberate reference environments, not a claim that they are the newest releases. Debian and SUSE differences are explained where they change administrative decisions. The common shell is Bash; the service manager is systemd. Commands specific to one family are labeled. Package versions, repository choices, enabled services, and organizational policies can change behavior even within one release.

Use the installed manual as the final authority for the installed program. Upstream documentation sometimes describes an option that an enterprise distribution has not shipped. Conversely, vendors may backport a fix without changing the major upstream version. The reference section links to original project documentation and distribution manuals. References support technical mechanisms; the operational scenarios, exercises, and example acceptance criteria are original teaching material.

The examples do not constitute a security certification or a guarantee that a machine is production-ready. In particular, a functioning single server is not a highly available service. The capstone identifies the additional approvals, identity integration, backup arrangements, monitoring, and recovery evidence needed before real use.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch001.xhtml — Technical scope

6. Safety and verification statement

Read-only examples and unprivileged companion tests can be run without changing system configuration. Privileged examples belong in disposable virtual machines until reviewed for a target environment. Storage formatting, account removal, firewall changes, boot changes, and fault injection are intentionally separated from ordinary inspection. Never run a chapter as one large pasted command block. Establish the preconditions for each operation first.

The companion’s test report describes the checks actually performed while preparing this edition. Syntax checks, fixture tests, EPUB validation, and document checks are not substitutes for a full two-distribution integration test. Privileged storage, SELinux, networking, cloud, and reboot procedures must be validated in the reader’s lab. Illustrative output is labeled as such and is not presented as a captured production result.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch001.xhtml — Safety and verification statement

7. Read for a decision, then trace the mechanism

Before entering a command, say what question it answers. df answers a different question from du. systemctl is-active answers a different question from an HTTP request. dig tests DNS directly, while getent follows the system’s name-service path. Memorizing these distinctions gives you something more useful than a list of command names: it gives you a way to choose the next test.

Each worked example follows a repeatable learning cycle. The requirement describes the outcome. The simplest approach exposes why a tempting shortcut fails. A mechanism view shows the relevant layers. The command walkthrough makes a small change. Evidence checks connect the result to the requirement. A recovery step closes the exercise. Read the explanations between code blocks; they establish which host, identity, directory, and state the commands assume.

When practicing, keep an operations notebook with the time, host, command, observation, hypothesis, and next action. Do not record private keys, passwords, tokens, or complete confidential log messages. A useful notebook preserves reasoning and reproducibility without becoming another secret store.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch002.xhtml — Read for a decision, then trace the mechanism

8. Lab topology and names

Use two virtual machines and, when available, a separate client. admin1 is your management workstation or control VM. web1 is the server you will configure. A second server, web2, is optional for networking, file sharing, and fleet exercises. Allocate roughly two virtual CPUs, 2–4 GiB of RAM, and a 25–40 GiB system disk to a basic VM, then adjust to your host’s available capacity. Those are teaching starting points, not production sizing guidance.

Use a host-only or isolated virtual network for service experiments and a separate NAT connection for package downloads. Do not expose lab SSH, NFS, SMB, or test web ports directly to the public internet. The sample network is 192.168.56.0/24; it must be changed if it conflicts with your existing networks. Example DNS names end in .test, such as status.harbor.test. Documentation addresses in 192.0.2.0/24, 198.51.100.0/24, or 203.0.113.0/24 are not usable internet destinations.

Take a clean VM snapshot after installation and updates. Keep a second recovery method, such as the hypervisor console and installation media. A snapshot is a convenient lab reset, not an independent backup. Attach a separately identified, disposable virtual disk for storage exercises. Do not practice partitioning on the system disk merely because the device name resembles the book’s example.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch002.xhtml — Lab topology and names

9. Command conventions · 1/2

Code blocks labeled bash contain shell commands. Commands do not include a decorative shell prompt, so they are easier to copy. A line beginning with # inside such a block is a comment, except for a script’s initial #!/usr/bin/env bash line. sudo marks an operation requiring elevated privileges. A command without sudo is intended for the current user unless the surrounding text explicitly states that you are in a root recovery shell.

A backslash at the end of a shell line continues the command onto the next line. It must be the last character; spaces after it change the meaning. Text such as LAB_DISK or CONNECTION_NAME is a variable whose value must first be established. Sample hostnames are not live endpoints. Configuration blocks are file contents, not commands to run at a shell prompt.

A command’s exit status is a small integer describing its result. Zero conventionally means success. Nonzero values need interpretation: for example, grep uses one for no match and two for an error. Capture $? immediately after the command you are examining. Running another command replaces it.

Privileges apply to processes, not to the visual appearance of a line. In sudo command > /etc/file, your current shell opens the destination before sudo runs. Use sudoedit for interactive configuration changes, or a reviewed sudo tee pipeline when writing a small, explicit configuration. The difference matters both for correctness and for avoiding accidental root-owned files.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch002.xhtml — Command conventions

10. Command conventions · 2/2

Section examples in this revision: Every numbered section in Chapters 1–33 ends with a Linux example and an explanation of what to check. Read the section first, then work through its example on the appropriate lab host. Shell commands are Bash unless another interpreter is explicitly named; configuration fragments belong in files, not directly at a shell prompt.

Run one distribution branch at a time. Debian/Ubuntu, RHEL-family, SUSE, SELinux, AppArmor, cloud, and container examples require their corresponding environment and installed tools. A commented command is illustrative syntax, not an action already performed. Uppercase names such as LAB_VM, LAB_PROFILE, and VERIFIED_LAB_ZONE must be replaced with positively verified lab values.

A block beginning with lab=$(mktemp -d) creates its own workspace and may replace a previous lab variable. Examples that refer to an earlier workspace or artifact say so explicitly; retain that exact path or repeat the named setup. Inspect temporary files before deleting them. Do not run the entire book as one script.

The examples are teaching procedures, not claims that every tool or workload was executed on every distribution. Shell syntax checks cannot verify package availability, service behavior, network access, filesystem support, or provider permissions. Privileged and state-changing steps require the disposable lab and recovery boundaries stated in the section.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch002.xhtml — Command conventions

11. Risk labels

Observe means the command is intended to inspect state. Reading some logs still requires permission and may expose sensitive information. Change means the operation modifies a reversible setting or file. Back up the exact configuration and establish a rollback. Destructive lab means the operation can erase data, interrupt access, or intentionally break a service. Run it only in a disposable VM with console access and an identified target.

These labels describe the examples, not a universal guarantee. An innocent-looking diagnostic can create load on a busy host, and a recursive search can cross into a slow network mount. Scope observation as carefully as change. A two-minute incident does not justify an unbounded command against every filesystem.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch002.xhtml — Risk labels

12. Reading paths

A new administrator should read Chapters 1–16 in order, then security and service administration in Chapters 17–21. Chapters 22–24 turn those fundamentals into a diagnostic method. Chapters 25–31 expand from one host to infrastructure. Chapters 32 and 33 are the assessment and capstone.

An experienced operator can begin with Chapters 23 and 32, identify weak layers, and return to the relevant foundations. A developer moving into operations should pay special attention to identity, service supervision, storage persistence, backup recovery, and change control. A successful deployment is only the beginning of a service’s operating life.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch002.xhtml — Reading paths

13. Companion package

The companion contains small Bash programs, systemd examples, NGINX configurations, an Ansible exercise, fixture-driven tests, and runbook templates. Appendix B prints the remaining core utility scripts and explains how to use these materials offline. Start with README.md, then read TEST_REPORT.md. Run the unprivileged test runner from the companion directory with bash tests/run_tests.sh. It must not be run with sudo.

The companion is intentionally not a universal bootstrap script. It does not partition arbitrary disks, rewrite SSH policy, open firewall ports, or turn a fresh cloud account into production infrastructure. Those tasks require decisions that cannot safely be guessed. A reliable example makes its boundaries visible instead of hiding them behind a one-line installer.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch002.xhtml — Companion package

14. Reading mechanism views

Text diagrams describe relationships, not hidden guarantees. An arrow from a client to a server means a request or dependency named in the caption. It does not imply authentication, encryption, redundancy, or automatic recovery unless those properties are explicitly shown. Several chapters return to the same request path because the location of a failure matters more than how complicated a diagram looks.

The central operating rule is simple: observe before changing, validate before applying, verify after applying, and test recovery before depending on it.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch002.xhtml — Reading mechanism views
